title: How Do Vitamin C Dose and Supplement Type Affect Tooth Growth?
text:
Does the amount of vitamin C and the type of supplement affect tooth growth?
In this analysis, I explore the ToothGrowth dataset in R to see how tooth growth changes with different vitamin C doses and supplement types. This data exploration looks at whether a higher dose leads to more tooth growth and whether orange juice (OJ) or ascorbic acid (VC) makes a difference.


The ToothGrowth dataset is built into R. The dataset contains tooth growth measurements from guinea pigs given different doses of vitamin C through either orange juice (OJ) or ascorbic acid (VC).
Data source: R datasets package documentation



Here I load the packages I need and take a look at the dataset.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

tooth_growth <- ToothGrowth

head(tooth_growth)

   len supp dose
1  4.2   VC  0.5
2 11.5   VC  0.5
3  7.3   VC  0.5
4  5.8   VC  0.5
5  6.4   VC  0.5
6 10.0   VC  0.5


I also check the structure of the dataset to see what variables I am working with.

str(tooth_growth)

'data.frame':   60 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ len : num  4.2 11.5 7.3 5.8 6.4 10 11.2 11.2 5.2 7 ...
 $ supp: Factor w/ 2 levels "OJ","VC": 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 ...
 $ dose: num  0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 ...





To see how tooth growth changes, I compare the average tooth length for each vitamin C dose and supplement type.

tooth_summary <- tooth_growth |>
  group_by(dose, supp) |>
  summarise(
    mean_tooth_growth = mean(len),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

tooth_summary

# A tibble: 6 × 3
   dose supp  mean_tooth_growth
  <dbl> <fct>             <dbl>
1   0.5 OJ                13.2 
2   0.5 VC                 7.98
3   1   OJ                22.7 
4   1   VC                16.8 
5   2   OJ                26.1 
6   2   VC                26.1 


The average tooth growth increases as the vitamin C dose increases for both supplement types.
At doses 0.5 and 1, orange juice (OJ) has a higher average tooth growth than ascorbic acid (VC). At dose 2, the average tooth growth is almost the same for both supplement types.
Dose has a strong relationship with tooth growth, while supplement type may matter more at lower doses.



To see the overall effect of dose more clearly, I compare the distribution of tooth growth across the three vitamin C dose levels.

ggplot(tooth_growth, aes(x = factor(dose), y = len)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Vitamin C dose",
    y = "Tooth growth",
    title = "Tooth Growth by Vitamin C Dose"
  )







Figure 1: Distribution of tooth growth across vitamin C dose levels.





The boxplot shows that tooth growth generally increases as the vitamin C dose increases.
The 0.5 dose has the lowest tooth growth values, while the 2.0 dose has the highest. There is still some variation within each dose group, but the overall pattern shows that higher doses are associated with greater tooth growth.



I compare tooth growth between orange juice (OJ) and ascorbic acid (VC) to see whether the supplement type makes a difference.

ggplot(tooth_growth, aes(x = supp, y = len)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Supplement type",
    y = "Tooth growth",
    title = "Tooth Growth by Supplement Type"
  )







Figure 2: Distribution of tooth growth by supplement type.





The boxplot shows that orange juice (OJ) generally has higher tooth growth than ascorbic acid (VC).
However, the two supplement types still overlap quite a lot. This suggests that supplement type alone does not drive tooth growth as much as vitamin C dose.



Since supplement type seems to matter differently at each dose, I compare both variables together.

ggplot(
  tooth_growth,
  aes(
    x = factor(dose),
    y = len,
    fill = supp
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
  labs(
    x = "Vitamin C dose",
    y = "Tooth growth",
    fill = "Supplement type",
    title = "Tooth Growth by Dose and Supplement Type"
  )







Figure 3: Tooth growth across vitamin C dose and supplement type.





The plot shows that tooth growth increases as the vitamin C dose increases for both supplement types.
At the lower doses of 0.5 and 1, orange juice (OJ) has higher tooth growth than ascorbic acid (VC). At dose 2, the two supplement types are much more similar.
This suggests that Vitamin C dose has the strongest overall relationship with tooth growth, while supplement type seems to matter more at lower doses.



Overall, tooth growth increases as the vitamin C dose increases.
Orange juice (OJ) generally shows higher tooth growth than ascorbic acid (VC) at the lower doses, but this difference becomes much smaller at the highest dose.
This analysis suggests that vitamin C dose has a stronger relationship with tooth growth than supplement type, although both appear to matter.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
A quiet afternoon on the UBC campus.


The first week was exciting yet full of challenges. Navigating where classes are and understanding how to retrieve and submit assignments were the most difficult parts. The pace was fast but I think by mid week two, I was able to adjust my time management. I have a good idea now on where I should be putting in more work to cover all the concepts. I also found some nice study spots in the koerner library where it’s really quiet. UBC is a big campus and there are still so many places to explore. Some of my favorite scenic places has to be the water fountain. I also like to grab coffee and some snacks in between lectures and enjoy the seasonal drinks. It’s a little self reward system that gives me something to look forward to in the day. It’s started to be a little chilly in the mornings and I caught a small cold. But as we are settling into new routines, I am really happy to be studying at such a beautiful campus. The rain hasn’t caught up to us yet, so its a great weather to be out and about.

title: Data Exploration with Palmer Penguins: Can physical measurements distinguish Penguin Species?
text:
Can we distinguish penguin species just by their physical measurements?
In this analysis, I explore the Palmer Penguins dataset to compare features such as body mass, flipper length, bill length, and bill depth. I investigate whether these measurements can help distinguish a penguin’s species and, if so, which feature appears to be the strongest indicator.

title: Data Exploration with Palmer Penguins: Can physical measurements distinguish Penguin Species?

title: Data Exploration with Palmer Penguins: Can physical measurements distinguish Penguin Species?
text:
Data
Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.
The dataset contains measurements for Adelie, Gentoo and Chinstrap penguins. The variables I explore are body mass, flipper length, bill length, and bill depth.

title: Data Exploration with Palmer Penguins: Can physical measurements distinguish Penguin Species?
text:
Data Aggregation
To determine whether the penguin species differ physically, I compare the average body mass, flipper length, bill length, and bill depth for each species.
I do this using Python’s groupby() and agg() functions to group observations by species and calculate the mean of each physical measurement.

species_summary = (
    penguins_clean
    .groupby("species")
    .agg(
        mean_body_mass=("body_mass_g", "mean"),
        mean_flipper_length=("flipper_length_mm", "mean"),
        mean_bill_length=("bill_length_mm", "mean"),
        mean_bill_depth=("bill_depth_mm", "mean")
    )
    .round(1)
)

title: Data Exploration with Palmer Penguins: Can physical measurements distinguish Penguin Species?
text:
Comparing Variable Distributions
The averages show some differences between the three penguin species, but they do not show how much the individual measurements overlap.
To find which physical feature may be the strongest indicator of species, I compare the distribution of each measurement across the three species.

penguins_clean.boxplot(
    column="flipper_length_mm",
    by="species"
)

plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Flipper length (mm)")
plt.title("Flipper Length by Penguin Species")
plt.suptitle("")

plt.show()







Figure 1: Distribution of flipper length across Palmer penguin species.





The boxplot shows that Gentoo penguins generally have much longer flippers than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins. However, Adelie and Chinstrap have a lot of overlap in their flipper lengths.
This suggests that flipper length may be a useful indicator for identifying Gentoo penguins, but it may not be enough to clearly distinguish between all three species.

title: Data Exploration with Palmer Penguins: Can physical measurements distinguish Penguin Species?
text:
Bill Length by Species
Next, I compare bill length across the species to see if it provides clearer separation.

penguins_clean.boxplot(
    column="bill_length_mm",
    by="species"
)

plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Bill length (mm)")
plt.title("Bill Length by Penguin Species")
plt.suptitle("")

plt.show()







Figure 2: Distribution of bill length across Palmer penguin species.





The plot shows that Adelie penguins generally have shorter bills than Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins. Still, Chinstrap and Gentoo have a lot of overlap in their bill lengths.
Bill length may be useful for identifying Adelie penguins, but it may not clearly distinguish between Chinstrap and Gentoo.

title: Data Exploration with Palmer Penguins: Can physical measurements distinguish Penguin Species?
text:
Bill Depth by Species
I compare bill depth across the three species to see whether it provides a clearer distinction.

penguins_clean.boxplot(
    column="bill_depth_mm",
    by="species"
)

plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Bill depth (mm)")
plt.title("Bill Depth by Penguin Species")
plt.suptitle("")

plt.show()







Figure 3: Distribution of bill depth across Palmer penguin species.





Gentoo penguins generally have shallower bills than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins. Adelie and Chinstrap have very similar bill depths and overlap heavily.
Bill depth may be useful for identifying Gentoo penguins, but it’s not enough to clearly distinguish between all three species.

title: Data Exploration with Palmer Penguins: Can physical measurements distinguish Penguin Species?
text:
Body Mass by Species
Finally, I compare body mass across the three species to see whether body size provides a clearer distinction.

penguins_clean.boxplot(
    column="body_mass_g",
    by="species"
)

plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Body mass (g)")
plt.title("Body Mass by Penguin Species")
plt.suptitle("")

plt.show()







Figure 4: Distribution of body mass across Palmer penguin species.





The plot shows that Gentoo penguins generally have a much higher body mass than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins. Adelie and Chinstrap have very similar body mass distributions and overlap heavily.
Body mass may be useful for identifying Gentoo penguins, but it is not enough to clearly distinguish between all three species.

title: Data Exploration with Palmer Penguins: Can physical measurements distinguish Penguin Species?
text:
Recap of the Analysis
So far, each individual feature has some limitations:

Flipper length: helps identify Gentoo penguins.
Body mass: helps identify Gentoo penguins.
Bill length: helps identify Adelie penguins.
Bill depth: helps identify Gentoo penguins.

No single measurement clearly separates all three species, so I next look at whether combining two measurements provides a clearer distinction.

title: Data Exploration with Palmer Penguins: Can physical measurements distinguish Penguin Species?
section: Combining Bill Length and Bill Depth
text:
Combining Bill Length and Bill Depth
I compare bill length and bill depth together to see whether using two measurements provides a clearer distinction.

for species, group in penguins_clean.groupby("species"):
    plt.scatter(
        group["bill_length_mm"],
        group["bill_depth_mm"],
        label=species,
        alpha=0.7
    )

plt.xlabel("Bill length (mm)")
plt.ylabel("Bill depth (mm)")
plt.title("Bill Length vs. Bill Depth by Penguin Species")
plt.legend(title="Species")

plt.show()







Figure 5: Bill length and bill depth across Palmer penguin species.





The scatterplot shows a much clearer separation between the three species when bill length and bill depth are considered together.
Adelie penguins generally have shorter bills with greater bill depth, while Gentoo penguins tend to have longer but shallower bills. Chinstrap penguins generally have longer and deeper bills.
There is still some overlap between individual penguins, but using both measurements together distinguishes the three species more clearly than using either measurement alone.

title: Data Exploration with Palmer Penguins: Can physical measurements distinguish Penguin Species?
text:
Conclusion
Overall, the plots show that one measurement alone is not enough to clearly separate all three species. Gentoo penguins are easier to identify using body mass, flipper length, and bill depth, while bill length helps separate Adelie. The clearest result came from looking at bill length and bill depth together.
This data exploration suggests that looking at a combination of physical features is a better indicator of penguin species than relying on a single feature.

title: About Me
text: I grew up in Myanmar and Thailand before moving abroad to pursue my bachelor’s degree in Data Science at James Cook University Singapore. Singapore shaped me as a person as I was leaving a collectivist culture into a more independent one. I made good friends, attended conferences and took part in data competitions. After university, working in banking taught me alot about the impact of finance and the importance of building good human relationships. Beyond my career, I also got my real estate license and worked as an independent real estate agent on the side. When the inflation crisis hit in Myanmar, what I learned about finance and investing became especially valuable, as I was able to help my family manage our finances through more strategic investments.

title: About Me
text:
Why Data
My passion in data led to me to this program. Choosing big data as a career has its fair share of challenges. There is a persistent need to upskill to keep up with real-time demands. I think of data as the infrastructure powering the front lines of innovation. Seeing different industries through the lens of data is insightful, fascinating and impactful. Working with data taught me to think more analytically and it has been a rewarding experience to continue learning and growing in this field.

title: About Me
text:
Life Besides Data
Outside of Data Science, I enjoy cooking and learning about buddhist philosophies. I’ve recently methodized grocery shopping based off universal pantry staples, staples based off cuisine, and niche ingredients for different recipes. Good food is the cure to almost everything, I believe. I grew up with mostly asian flavors and cusines and they are a great comfort meal for whenever I’m feeling homesick. Cooking at home is also more nutritious. I’ve been learning more about medicinal ingredients and sharing my findings with my mom back home. On the weekends I like to plan for recipes and make my own versions. When the day ends, I like to medidate before going to bed. I think alot about inner peace, compassion and human sufferings. As I’ve had to live through war in my home country, these values have helped me to process difficult experiences and rethink what gives life meaning.
